title: Earn Just Over £100k? You Keep 38p of Each Extra £1 🪤💷 #shorts
description:
Earn just over £100,000 and you keep only 38p of each extra pound.

Between £100,000 and £125,140 your tax-free Personal Allowance (£12,570) shrinks by £1 for every £2 you earn over £100,000. So each extra £1 costs 40p in higher-rate tax, plus 20p on the allowance you lose (50p of allowance taxed at 40%), plus 2p National Insurance: 62p gone, 38p kept.

The fix people miss: on a £110,000 salary, £10,000 paid into a pension brings your adjusted net income back to £100,000, and the whole allowance comes back. With relief at source you pay in £8,000, the provider adds £2,000, and you claim £4,000 back on your tax return, so £10,000 in your pension costs you £4,000. The catch: the higher-rate part isn't automatic, you claim it through Self Assessment.

Sources: gov.uk/income-tax-rates · gov.uk/income-tax-rates/income-over-100000 · gov.uk/guidance/adjusted-net-income · gov.uk/tax-on-your-private-pension/pension-tax-relief · gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-thresholds-for-employers-2026-to-2027

Illustration only. 2026/27 rates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland's income tax bands differ). Employee, category A National Insurance. Ignores student loans and other income. Pension contributions count towards your annual allowance. General education, not financial advice.
